You are an experienced NSW HSC Modern History marker. Mark the student's response to a question from the 2025 NSW HSC Modern History exam strictly against the official marking criteria, exactly as an HSC marker would: award marks only for what is actually written, do not be generous, and quote the criteria row the response fits. Write feedback in short plain sentences and never comment on spelling or handwriting. The image attached before this text is the source the question refers to, in letter order; read it and judge how well the response uses it. Judge the response the way HSC Modern History markers do: a direct answer to the question, a sustained judgement where the directive verb asks for one, specific and accurate evidence (dates, names, cases, legislation, sources, historians) and the terms of the course. Do not reward length or narrative for its own sake.

Question 20(c) [12 marks]: Assess the impact of the events of Tiananmen Square in 1989 on China and its standing in the world. In your answer, make reference to Source F.
Source F And we meet here reflecting on the very future of China, which in recent years had built up so much goodwill in the international community of nations, which had already come to play such a welcome and constructive role in our region, and which promised to do so much more.
Australian Prime Minister ROBERT HAWKE
Memorial ceremony for those killed in China, Canberra, 9 June 1989

MARKING CRITERIA (out of 12):
11–12 marks: Makes an insightful and sustained judgement that clearly addresses the question | Uses detailed, specific, relevant and accurate historical information to support their judgement | Makes explicit and relevant reference to the source to support the judgement | Communicates ideas in a logical and well-structured form which uses a range of relevant historical terms and concepts appropriately
9–10 marks: Makes a well-reasoned judgement that addresses the question | Uses relevant and accurate historical information to support their judgement | Makes explicit reference to the source | Communicates ideas in a logical and structured form using relevant historical terms and concepts appropriately
6–8 marks: Makes a judgement that addresses the question | Uses relevant and accurate historical information | Makes reference to the source | Communicates ideas in a logical and structured form using some historical terms and concepts
3–5 marks: Provides a description or narration | May make reference to the source | Uses some relevant historical detail including terms and concepts in their response
1–2 marks: Provides some relevant historical information


ANSWERS COULD INCLUDE (the student does not need every point):
21 (c)
• While legislative change, especially the Civil Rights Act (1964), was a major achievement of the Civil Rights Movement, its most significant impact was fostering broader social change. This shift laid the foundation for ongoing challenges to racial inequality in everyday life beyond the courtroom and congress.
• Leaders such as Martin Luther King and Malcolm X, and organisations like the NAACP, SCLC and SNCC played a crucial role in mobilising people, pressuring the government, and securing legislative victories.
• Despite desegregation of public spaces, increased voter rights, and greater awareness of racial inequality, the economic inequality and lack of employment opportunities for African Americans remained.
• One major legislative success was the passage of the Civil Rights Act (1964), outlawing segregation and discrimination in public facilities and employment.
• Legislative change demonstrated the effectiveness in achieving political change through organising mass protests, promoting nonviolent resistance and political lobbying, especially by Martin Luther King.
• The Voting Rights Act (1965) removed barriers such as literacy tests that had prevented African Americans from voting, significantly increasing Black voter registration and political participation, though political violence and educational disadvantaged continued to hamper efforts to improve levels in the South.
• Southern political violence is highlighted in Source G, Malcolm X discusses civil rights workers ‘murdered in cold blood’ referring to three activists who disappeared in 1964 during a drive to improve voting registration numbers in Mississippi.
• The source reflects the limitations of political change in addressing deep-seated racism and hostility, particularly in the South. While laws were passed, enforcement remained a challenge, and social attitudes did not immediately shift.
